newsitem.title: INDIA: Indian lawmakers upbraid government over WTO talks.
newsitem.headline: Indian lawmakers upbraid government over WTO talks.

text.p: Irate lawmakers demanding a government statement on India's stance at world trade talks forced the abrupt adjournment of both houses of parliament on Friday.

Members hit out at Prime Minister H.D. Deve Gowda's minority coalition, saying the government had caved in under Western pressure over the sensitive issue of labour standards at the meeting of the World Trade Organisation in Singapore.
"It is a black day for India," news agencies quoted opposition leader Atal Bihari Vajpayee of the right-wing Bharatiya Janata Party as saying.

The speaker of the lower house, P.A. Sangma, demanded that the government provide full details of negotiations over labour standards and investment before India signed the WTO declaration in Singapore.

Newspapers said India had softened its stance at the Singapore meeting over labour standards and investment. "India falls in line on labour norms, WTO investment study", The Economic Times said in a headline.
India had opposed linking trade and labour, arguing that rich nations aimed to erect trade barriers in the name of labour standards to protect their industries.
"Things have changed and things are changing," the Press Trust of India (PTI) quoted Sangma as saying.

"We have surrendered to U.S. pressure at the cost of our sovereignty," PTI quoted Rupchand Pal of the Communist Party of India-Marxist (CPI-M) as saying. The CPI-M supports Deve Gowda's centre-left coalition but is not in the government.

PTI quoted Finance Minister P. Chidambaram as saying the "situation (in Singapore) is evolving", but that "members will be fully satisfied that the position taken by India is fully consistent with its stated position".
Ministers and officials from 128 countries adopted a final declaration at the end of the five-day WTO conference on Friday.
On the contentious labour issue, ministers declared they had renewed their "commitment to the observance of internationally recognised core labour standards".
But they said the United Nations' International Labour Organisation was the "competent body to set a deal on these standards", which could not be used for protectionist purposes.
